q: How much does it cost to clear a sample?
a: There is no rate card. A clearance agent reported publishing fees of about $1,500 to $2,500 and master fees of $1,500 to $10,000 in 2018, and an attorney's rough 2026 range was $2,000 to $10,000 per side plus a 3% to 10% master royalty and up to 50% of the publishing. Famous cases run far higher: the Beastie Boys' "Paul's Boutique" clearances were reported at over $250,000 in 1989.

q: Do I need to clear a sample if it is under 7 seconds?
a: The US Copyright Office labels the idea that seven seconds or less is always fair use as fiction and says there is no formula. It says a sample usually needs the recording owner's permission and often the song owner's too, and that only a court decides fair use.

q: What is the difference between a sample and an interpolation?
a: A sample uses part of an existing recording. An interpolation re-records part of an existing song without the original audio, so, the US Copyright Office says, it needs the song owner's permission and not the recording owner's.

q: What happens if I release a song with an uncleared sample?
a: Practitioners say the owner can require the song to be pulled and that there is no exemption for non-commercial releases. Publisher Mara Kuge says that once the record is out, the artist has no leverage. One clearance agent says she has cleared remix albums about 10 years after release.

q: How long does sample clearance take?
a: Clearance agent Deborah Mannis-Gardner has seen it take from one day to over a year, and publisher Mara Kuge advises allowing at least a couple of months. Clearing De La Soul's first six albums for streaming took about a year.

q: Are Splice samples really royalty-free, and can I get a Content ID claim for using them?
a: Splice's license is royalty-free, non-exclusive and perpetual, and it survives canceling the subscription, but the buyer does not own the sound and cannot redistribute it as a sample or loop. Splice says it cannot guarantee a track will not be flagged by Content ID and issues a certified license for disputing claims. DistroKid says tracks built on such loops are ineligible for its Content ID add-on.

q: Why did The Verve lose the royalties to "Bitter Sweet Symphony"?
a: According to the band's manager, the recording was cleared with Decca but the publishing was sought late, after copies were pressed. ABKCO took 100% of the publishing and Richard Ashcroft was paid a reported $1,000. In 2019 Mick Jagger and Keith Richards signed their share over to him.

q: Why was De La Soul not on Spotify until 2023?
a: The group's first six albums had never been legally available digitally, and an earlier clearance effort stalled amid a dispute with the label. After Reservoir Media bought the catalog, clearance restarted in January 2022 and the albums reached streaming on March 3, 2023, with replays and interpolations used on a handful of songs.
